# Kappa calculus

`kappa-calculus` · *Danos & Laneve, 2004; the Kappa language: Danos, Feret, Fontana, Harmer, Krivine et al., 2007 onwards*

*Also known as:* *κ-calculus*, *Kappa*, *Kappa language*, *rule-based modelling of site graphs*

## Introduction

Kappa is a language for writing down how proteins bind to each other and
modify each other, without having to list every molecule that can result. A
protein is drawn as a node with a few named *sites*, the patches through which
it binds partners or carries a chemical mark such as a phosphate. A *rule*
says what happens to a small fragment of a complex, for example "an A that is
already bound to something can bind a free, unphosphorylated C", and says
nothing about the rest. Because the rule ignores everything it does not
mention, it applies to every complex that contains the fragment. One rule is
therefore a whole family of chemical reactions, and a handful of rules can
stand for thousands.

That is the problem Kappa was built for. Signalling proteins have many sites,
and each site can be free, bound or modified, so the number of distinct
complexes grows combinatorially. Danos and Laneve (2004) say it plainly: what
they want to express is "the combinatorics of the interaction between
proteins". Their paper, *Formal molecular biology*, introduced the κ-calculus
(kappa calculus) as a process algebra, one of the formal languages computer
scientists use to describe concurrent systems, applied to proteins: "a
particular restricted kind of graph-rewriting operating on graph-with-sites".
They illustrated it on a simplified signalling pathway and on the lactose
operon of *E. coli*. The paper had no rates yet ("for now we don't have such a
quantitative semantics"). The calculus then grew into the Kappa language, with
a stochastic simulator (KaSim), a compiler to differential equations (KaDE)
and a reference guide by Fontana, Boutillier, Feret and Krivine, which
describes Kappa as a rule-based modelling language for "systems of
interacting structured entities".

Kappa is a **formalism**: a notation with an exact meaning, not a model of a
particular system. A Kappa model is a set of signatures (which agents exist
and what sites they have), rules with rate constants, and an initial mixture.
The same idea, organic chemistry's habit of writing a reaction mechanism as a
rewrite of a structural fragment, is carried over from atoms and valences to
proteins and binding sites.

Banzhaf and Yamamoto give it one paragraph in §9.7, "Other Formal Calculi
Inspired by a Chemical Metaphor", next to [Brane calculi](brane-calculi.md):
objects are proteins, rules express binding into complexes and dissociation
from them, complexes are graphs, and rules are graph-rewriting rules. They
note it "has been used to model gene regulation, signal transduction, and
protein-protein interaction networks in general". Its catalog neighbours
differ in what they rewrite. Brane calculi rewrite the nesting of membranes,
not the bonds between proteins. [MGS](mgs.md) rewrites collections with a
neighbourhood topology (sequences, grids). [ToyChem](toychem.md) rewrites
molecular graphs of atoms and bonds and computes energies; Kappa has no
energies, only rate constants. [SRSim](srsim.md) uses rules of the same kind
but places molecules in three-dimensional space, which Kappa does not.
Compared with the textbook [dimerization](dimerization.md) network, where each
species is a bare name, Kappa's species have visible structure, and that
structure is what lets one rule cover many reactions.

| at a glance | |
|---|---|
| **family** | rewriting |
| **kind** | formalism |
| **type** | generator — an algorithm computes the network from the chemistry's arguments |
| **constructive** | yes — the species set grows at run time |
| **fidelity** | `reconstructed` — built from the original papers listed under *References* |
| **book** | 9.7 |
| **provides** | `topology`, `stoichiometry`, `rate-constants`, `initial-state`, `mass-conservation`, `sequence-structure-function` |

## How it works

### Agents, sites and complexes

An **agent** is one protein molecule. Its type and its sites are declared in a
**signature**. The default model, the "Hello ABC" example of the reference
guide (§1.3), declares three:

```
A(x,c)                 an A with two binding sites, x and c
B(x)                   a B with one binding site, x
C(x1{u p},x2{u p})     a C with two sites, each unphosphorylated (u) or phosphorylated (p)
```

Every site has a **link state**: free, written `[.]`, or bound, written with a
bond number `[1]` that appears exactly twice, once at each end of the bond. A
site may also carry an **internal state** in braces, such as `{u}` or `{p}`,
standing for a chemical modification. A **complex** is a set of agents joined
by bonds into one connected graph. Each complex, written with every site
spelled out, is one species of the network:

```
A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.])
```

This is an A bound to a B through their `x` sites (bond 1) and to a C through
its `c` site and C's `x1` site (bond 2); C is still unphosphorylated on both
sites and `x2` is free. The same complex could be written with the agents in
another order or the bonds numbered differently. Chemart rewrites every
complex into one **canonical** text, so that two writings of the same graph
(two *isomorphic* site graphs) are the same species.

### Rules are patterns, not reactions

A rule has a left-hand side, a right-hand side and a rate. Its sides are
**patterns**: partial site graphs that mention only the sites that matter.
Rule 2 of the ABC model reads:

```
'rule 2' A(x[_],c[.]), C(x1{u}[.]) -> A(x[_],c[2]), C(x1{u}[2]) @ 1.0E-4
```

In words: an A whose site `x` is bound to anything (`[_]`) and whose site `c`
is free binds a C whose site `x1` is free and unphosphorylated; the new bond
joins A's `c` to C's `x1`. C's second site `x2` is not written, so its state
does not matter. The reference guide makes the point: "This is why a rule is
not a reaction... a rule subsumes many possible reactions."

A rule applies wherever its left-hand side can be found in a complex. Finding
it means an **embedding**: a one-to-one map from the pattern's agents to
agents of the mixture that respects types, the states written in the pattern
and its bonds. The five ABC rules say, in order: A and B bind and come apart
again (rule 1, reversible, with a forward and a backward rate); an A bound to
B binds unphosphorylated C (rule 2); an A bound to C phosphorylates C's `x1`
and lets go (rule 3); a *free* A binds C on `x2` once `x1` is phosphorylated
(rule 4); and phosphorylates `x2` and lets go (rule 5). All the rule
applications change only bonds and internal states; no agent is ever created
or destroyed.

### From rules to a reaction network

Kappa's own simulator, KaSim, never lists species. It keeps the whole mixture
as one big graph, tracks every embedding of every rule, and fires rules one at
a time in continuous-time Monte Carlo (the Gillespie algorithm). Chemart works
differently: it **flattens** the rules into the equivalent ordinary reaction
network, the one KaDE (Camporesi, Feret and Lý, 2017) computes. Starting from
the initial complexes, it tries every rule on every complex and pair of
complexes, adds the products as new species, and repeats until nothing new
appears. The set reached is the *closure* of the rules over the initial
mixture.

Here is what rule 2 becomes in the default network. Only one complex in the
closure contains an A bound on `x` and free on `c`, namely the AB dimer, and
only one contains a free unphosphorylated `x1`, the fresh C. So rule 2 yields
one reaction:

```
C(x1{u}[.],x2{u}[.]) + A(x[1],c[.]),B(x[1]) -> A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.])  [mass-action k=0.0001]
```

Rule 1 is the opposite case. It asks only for an A free on `x` and a B free on
`x`, and three different complexes contain such an A: the bare A, A bound to C
on `x1`, and A bound to C on `x2`. Rule 1 therefore yields three binding
reactions (rates left out here), and its reverse three unbinding reactions:

```
A(x[.],c[.]) + B(x[.]) -> A(x[1],c[.]),B(x[1])                                                    rule 1
B(x[.]) + A(x[.],c[1]),C(x1{u}[1],x2{u}[.]) -> A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.])          rule 1
B(x[.]) + A(x[.],c[1]),C(x1{p}[.],x2{u}[1]) -> A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{p}[.],x2{u}[2])          rule 1
```

Six rule directions (five rules, one reversible) give 11 reactions over 10
complexes. Each reaction gets a mass-action rate constant computed from the
rule's rate and the number of ways the rule can produce it, so that the
reaction's rate equals the rule's *activity*, the quantity KaSim uses to
choose which rule fires.

### Molecularity: one complex or two

A rule whose left-hand side has two disconnected parts, like rule 2 (an A and
a C), could in principle match both parts inside a single complex. Following
KaDE, Chemart matches the parts in two *different* complexes, a bimolecular
reaction, unless the rule gives a second, unimolecular rate in braces,
`@ k {k_uni}`. The reference guide's polymerisation rule shows why the
distinction matters:

```
'ambiguous molecularity' A(x[.]), A(y[.]) -> A(x[1]), A(y[1]) @ 0.001 {0.1}
```

Joining two chains end to end is a collision between two molecules (rate
0.001); joining the two ends of *one* chain closes it into a ring and needs no
collision (rate 0.1). The two rates scale differently with volume, which is
why the guide asks for both.

### Symmetry

When a pattern is symmetric, the same match can be found in several ways, and
a convention is needed for how many times to count it. The guide's example is
two rules on a symmetric dimer of two unphosphorylated A's:

```
'1p' A(x[1]{u}), A(x[1]{u}) -> A(x[1]{p}), A(x[1]{u}) @ k      phosphorylate one of the two
'2p' A(x[1]{u}), A(x[1]{u}) -> A(x[1]{p}), A(x[1]{p}) @ k      phosphorylate both
```

The guide describes three stances. *Stance D* (deterministic) counts the
symmetries of the left side that survive on the right: `'1p'` then has two
reaction centres (either A can be the one phosphorylated) and fires twice as
often as `'2p'`. *Stance ND* (non-deterministic, the usual convention of the
stochastic simulation algorithm) counts only the symmetries of the left side,
so the two rules fire equally often. *Null*, KaSim's default, ignores symmetry.
The guide adds that "nothing in Kappa hinges formally on how symmetries are
viewed"; the choice only rescales rate constants.

The formal specification below condenses this: S is the set of complexes, R
the rules read as reaction schemes, and A the ways the flattened network can
be run: as rate equations (ODE), stochastically (SSA), or as graph rewriting
in the manner of KaSim.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*implicit* — defined by a construction rule rather than listed). agents (proteins) with named sites; a site may carry an internal state (e.g. u/p) and a link to one site of another agent. A species is a complex: a connected, fully specified site graph, identified up to isomorphism. Species id and structure are its canonical Kappa expression, e.g. A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.])

Kappa site graphs are rigid (site names are distinct within an agent), so an embedding of a connected pattern is fixed by the image of one agent and the canonical form is the least breadth-first text over the possible roots.

**R — reactions** (*implicit* — computed by an algorithm from the molecules that meet; molecules per reaction: 1, 2). rules rewrite patterns (partially specified site graphs) by binding, unbinding and changing internal states, e.g. 'rule 2' A(x[_],c[.]), C(x1{u}[.]) -&gt; A(x[_],c[2]), C(x1{u}[2]) @ 1e-4. One rule stands for every reaction between complexes that contain its left-hand side; the network is the closure of the rules over the complexes reachable from the initial ones.

Components of a rule's left-hand side match distinct complexes (bimolecular); inside one complex only when a unimolecular rate is given (@ k {k_uni}). Rules with three or more disconnected components give reactions of that order.

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time); or `ssa` (stochastic simulation (Gillespie): individual reaction events happen at random times); or `graph-rewrite` (graph rewriting: molecules are graphs and reactions rewrite them).

*How the population is bounded:* none

Kappa's native semantics is a continuous-time Monte Carlo over the site graph (KaSim) that never enumerates species; Chemart flattens the rules into the equivalent mass-action reaction network (KaDE's differential semantics), cut by species and complex-size budgets when polymerisation makes it infinite. The unflattened model is kept in extras (rules, signatures, init, kappa file text).

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("kappa-calculus", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
kappa-calculus: 10 species, 11 reactions, status=complete
provides: initial-state, mass-conservation, rate-constants, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: analysis, conservation, init, kappa, model, rate_convention, reaction_rules, rules, signatures, species_encoding
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
A(x[.],c[.]) + B(x[.]) -> A(x[1],c[.]),B(x[1])  [mass-action k=0.0001]
A(x[1],c[.]),B(x[1]) -> A(x[.],c[.]) + B(x[.])  [mass-action k=0.1]
C(x1{u}[.],x2{u}[.]) + A(x[1],c[.]),B(x[1]) -> A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.])  [mass-action k=0.0001]
A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.]) -> A(x[.],c[1]),C(x1{u}[1],x2{u}[.]) + B(x[.])  [mass-action k=0.1]
A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.]) -> A(x[1],c[.]),B(x[1]) + C(x1{p}[.],x2{u}[.])  [mass-action k=1.0]
A(x[.],c[1]),C(x1{u}[1],x2{u}[.]) -> A(x[.],c[.]) + C(x1{p}[.],x2{u}[.])  [mass-action k=1.0]
B(x[.]) + A(x[.],c[1]),C(x1{u}[1],x2{u}[.]) -> A(x[1],c[2]),B(x[1]),C(x1{u}[2],x2{u}[.])  [mass-action k=0.0001]
A(x[.],c[.]) + C(x1{p}[.],x2{u}[.]) -> A(x[.],c[1]),C(x1{p}[.],x2{u}[1])  [mass-action k=0.0001]
… and 3 more
```

The default call above flattens the ABC model: the 10 complexes and 11
reactions discussed under *How it works*, with the guide's rates (binding
`1e-4` per molecule per second, unbinding `0.1` and modification `1` per
second) and its initial mixture of 1,000 free A's, 1,000 free B's and 10,000
unmodified C's in `net.initial_state`. Species names are canonical Kappa
expressions; `Species.structure` is the same text.

The unflattened model stays with the network, so it can be handed to Kappa's
own tools:

- `net.extras["rules"]`, `["signatures"]`, `["init"]`: the model as given;
  `net.extras["kappa"]` is the same as a Kappa file (`%agent:` lines, rules,
  `%init:` lines).
- `net.extras["reaction_rules"]`: for each reaction, the labels of the rules
  that produce it (a reverse direction is labelled `'rule 1_op'`).
- `net.extras["conservation"]`: one conservation law per agent type, the
  number of agents of that type in each species. Since no rule creates or
  destroys agents, these totals never change.
- `net.extras["rate_convention"]`: the symmetry stance and each rule's
  symmetry counts. `net.extras["analysis"]` gives the largest complex and
  whether the size budget cut the network.

Chemart has no simulator of its own. To run the network, integrate its
mass-action equations. This script does so and sums the complexes into the
four observables the guide plots in its figure 3:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import chemart

def simulate(net, t_eval):
    ids, R, P = net.matrices()
    R = R.toarray()
    S = (P.toarray() - R).astype(float)
    k = np.array([r.rate["k"] for r in net.reactions])
    x0 = np.array([net.initial_state.get(s, 0.0) for s in ids])
    f = lambda t, x: S @ (k * np.prod(x[:, None] ** R, axis=0))   # mass action
    sol = solve_ivp(f, (0, t_eval[-1]), x0, t_eval=t_eval, method="LSODA", rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-8)
    return dict(zip(ids, sol.y))

net = chemart.generate_network("kappa-calculus")
t = [1, 5, 20, 50, 100, 250]
x = simulate(net, t)
total = lambda pred: sum(v for s, v in x.items() if pred(s))
obs = {"AB":  total(lambda s: "B(x[1])" in s),
       "Cuu": total(lambda s: "C(x1{u}" in s and "x2{u}" in s),
       "Cpu": total(lambda s: "C(x1{p}" in s and "x2{u}" in s),
       "Cpp": total(lambda s: "C(x1{p}" in s and "x2{p}" in s)}
print("t     " + "".join(f"{n:>8}" for n in obs))
for i, ti in enumerate(t):
    print(f"{ti:<6}" + "".join(f"{v[i]:8.0f}" for v in obs.values()))
```

```
t           AB     Cuu     Cpu     Cpp
1           87    9990      10       0
5          270    9649     327      24
20         378    7295    1857     849
50         382    3772    2258    3971
100        382     959    1006    8036
250        382       4       7    9989
```

`AB` counts every A bound to a B, whatever else is attached, as the guide's
observable `|A(x[x.B])|` does. Unmodified C (`Cuu`) is replaced first by singly
modified C (`Cpu`), which peaks and falls, then by doubly modified C (`Cpp`).

**The EGFR network.** `model="egfr"` loads the model of early signalling by
the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) of Blinov et al. (2006), in the
Kappa translation shipped with KaDE's benchmarks. It has five agent types
(the ligand `egf`, the receptor `egfr`, and the adapter and signalling proteins
`Grb2`, `Shc` and `Sos`) and 23 rules, 16 of them reversible, labelled `R1` to
`R23`. It is the slow setting: about 16 seconds.

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("kappa-calculus", model="egfr")
print(net.summary().splitlines()[0])        # kappa-calculus: 356 species, 3749 reactions, status=complete
net.extras["analysis"]["largest_complex"]   # 14
```

Most of the 3,749 reactions come from a few general rules. The receptor
dimerisation rule `R2` and its reverse produce 300 reactions each, because a
receptor can dimerise whatever is attached to its other sites. At the other
extreme, rules `R19` to `R23`, which act on Shc, Grb2 and Sos away from the
receptor, produce one reaction per direction.

**Dimers and polymers.** The guide's section 2.3.1.1 contrasts two binding
rules. `model="dimerization"` binds two A's through the same site, so the
closure stops at the dimer:

```
kappa-calculus: 2 species, 1 reactions, status=complete
2 A(x[.]) -> A(x[1]),A(x[1])  [mass-action k=0.0005]
```

The rate is half the rule's `0.001` because the pattern is symmetric (see
*Symmetry*). `model="polymerization"` binds site `x` of one A to site `y` of
another, so chains can grow for ever, and the unimolecular rate closes them
into rings. The network is infinite, so `max_complex_size` cuts it; with
`max_complex_size=4` it has chains of 1 to 4 agents, rings of 2 to 4 and 7
reactions, and `status` is `truncated`. With the default size of 20 it has 39
species and 119 reactions.

**Symmetry conventions.** Pass `symmetry="rule"` (stance D, the default),
`"lhs"` (stance ND) or `"none"` (KaSim's Null). For the rules `'1p'` and
`'2p'` above, with `k = 1`, the flattened rate constants are:

```
rule {'1p': 2.0, '2p': 1.0}
lhs  {'1p': 1.0, '2p': 1.0}
none {'1p': 2.0, '2p': 2.0}
```

**Your own model.** With `model="custom"`, give `signatures`, `rules` and
`init` in Kappa 4 syntax (the first state listed in a signature is the
default). A kinase K that binds a substrate S and phosphorylates it:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network(
    "kappa-calculus", model="custom",
    signatures=["K(s)", "S(y{u p})"],
    rules=["'bind' K(s[.]), S(y{u}[.]) <-> K(s[1]), S(y{u}[1]) @ 1e-3, 0.1",
           "'cat' K(s[1]), S(y{u}[1]) -> K(s[.]), S(y{p}[.]) @ 1"],
    init={"K()": 100, "S()": 1000})
```

```
kappa-calculus: 4 species, 3 reactions, status=complete
K(s[.]) + S(y{u}[.]) -> K(s[1]),S(y{u}[1])  [mass-action k=0.001] ['bind']
K(s[1]),S(y{u}[1]) -> K(s[.]) + S(y{u}[.])  [mass-action k=0.1] ['bind_op']
K(s[1]),S(y{u}[1]) -> K(s[.]) + S(y{p}[.])  [mass-action k=1.0] ['cat']
```

Rules may also be written in Kappa's *edit notation*, `A(x[./1]),B(x[./1]) @ k`
(before/after in each slot). Chemart implements only part of Kappa: agent
creation and deletion, counters, tokens, named variables and rate
expressions are rejected with a `ValueError`, so rates must be plain numbers.
`max_species` and `max_complex_size` in the table below bound the closure.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `model` | `enum` | `abc` | structural | abc: the 'Hello ABC' model of the Kappa reference guide (sec. 1.3; 10 species, 11 reactions); dimerization: its 'symmetric dimerization' rule (sec. 2.3.1.1); polymerization: its 'ambiguous molecularity' rule A(x[.]),A(y[.]) -&gt; A(x[1]),A(y[1]) @ 0.001 {0.1} (chains and rings, truncated); egfr: the EGFR network of Blinov et al. (2006) from KaDE's benchmark egfr_net.ka (356 species, 3749 reactions); custom: signatures, rules and init <br>one of `abc`, `dimerization`, `polymerization`, `egfr`, `custom` |
| `signatures` | `list` | `[]` | structural | custom only: agent signatures, Kappa 4 syntax Name(site{state state ...}, ...) <br>*range:* e.g. ['A(x,c)', 'B(x)', 'C(x1{u p},x2{u p})']; the first state listed is the default |
| `rules` | `list` | `[]` | kinetic | custom only: Kappa rules with numeric rates; links [.] [n] [_] [#] [site.Agent], states {s} {#}, unwritten sites untested; agent creation and deletion are not supported <br>*range:* e.g. ["'bind' A(x[.]), B(x[.]) &lt;-&gt; A(x[1]), B(x[1]) @ 1e-4, 0.1"]; edit notation A(x[./1]),B(x[./1]) @ k; unimolecular rate as @ k {k_uni} |
| `init` | `dict` | `{}` | population | custom only: initial copies of each Kappa expression (its connected components are the initial complexes; unwritten sites take the default state and are free) <br>*range:* e.g. {'A(),B()': 1000, 'C(x1{u},x2{u})': 10000} |
| `symmetry` | `enum` | `rule` | kinetic | symmetry factor applied to rule rates (Kappa reference guide 3.3.1): rule = 1/\|automorphisms of the left-hand side preserved on the right\| (stance D, the biochemist convention), lhs = 1/\|Aut(L)\| (stance ND, the SSA convention), none = 1 (KaSim's default) <br>one of `rule`, `lhs`, `none` |
| `max_species` | `int` | `2000` | structural | species budget of the closure; reactions that would add more are dropped and status becomes truncated <br>`1` … `100000` · *range:* egfr closes at 356 species |
| `max_complex_size` | `int` | `20` | structural | maximum agents in a complex; reactions producing a larger complex are dropped and status becomes truncated (KaDE's truncation option) <br>`1` … `1000` · *range:* the largest egfr complex has 14 agents; polymerization closes only under this budget |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "11 decisions"

    - Language: the book's one paragraph and Danos & Laneve (2004) define the κ-calculus with sites that are bound, or free and visible or hidden. Chemart implements the subset of its successor, the Kappa 4 language of the reference guide, that covers exactly binding, unbinding and internal-state change: visible/hidden is an internal state {v h}. The 2004 paper's pdftotext extraction lost its Greek and symbols, so its algebraic syntax was not reproduced; the semantics (proteins with sites, complexes as connected graphs, complexation/decomplexation rules) is the same.
    - Not supported (ValueError): agent creation and deletion ('.' slots, + and - in edit notation), counters, tokens, %var names and algebraic rate expressions (rates are numbers). Hence agents of every type are conserved, given in extras.conservation.
    - v1 parameters agent_signatures (callable), rules (callable) and rates (matrix) became the model choice plus the custom signatures/rules/init lists in Kappa syntax, with rates written in the rules. Added symmetry, max_species and max_complex_size.
    - Flattening follows KaDE's differential semantics: each connected component of a rule's left-hand side matches its own complex; both components of a two-component rule match inside one complex only when a unimolecular rate {k} is given (KaSim instead applies a single rate to both cases). Rules with three or more components give only reactions of that order.
    - Rate of a flattened reaction R: k_R = sum over the embeddings of the rule into the reactant copies that yield R of gamma * Omega / prod m_i!, in molecule-count units with volume 1 (the rule rates of the published models are already per molecule). Then k_R prod x_i^m_i equals the rule activity of reference guide eq. (1), e.g. gamma n(n-1) for an A + A rule under 'none'. Reactions produced by several rules sum their rates; extras.reaction_rules lists the rules.
    - Symmetry convention default: 'rule' (stance D, 1/|Aut(L) preserved in R|), argued for in the reference guide's appendix E and named the biochemist convention by KaDE; 'lhs' (stance ND, SSA) and 'none' (KaSim's default, Null) are offered. The guide's prose says both '1p' and '2p' have activity k/2 under stance ND, but its eq. (1)-(2) give 2 embeddings x 1/2 x k = k; Chemart follows the equations, and the ratios the guide states ('1p' twice '2p' under D, and twice itself under ND) hold.
    - Species identity: the canonical Kappa expression (least breadth-first text over roots of the smallest agent type, sites in signature order, bonds numbered by appearance) is both id and structure, so isomorphic complexes are one species regardless of how they are written.
    - Named models: abc is the reference guide's section 1.3 model with its %var rates (on 1e-4, off 0.1, mod 1) and %init (1000 A, 1000 B, 10000 C); dimerization and polymerization are single rules printed in section 2.3.1.1 without initial amounts, so their initial_state is omitted (the seed is the free monomer). egfr translates KaDE's egfr_net.ka (Kappa 3: a bare site is free, site~state!link) programmatically into Kappa 4 with its %var values substituted; signatures are read off its %init lines; rules are labelled R1..R22 in file order.
    - Published counts reproduced: egfr gives 356 species and 3749 reactions, the numbers of Blinov et al. (2006) and of KaDE's ground network. The ABC network (10 species, 11 reactions) is not counted in the sources; it was derived by hand from the five rules and agrees with the generator.
    - Truncation: max_complex_size drops reactions whose products exceed it (KaDE offers the same truncation); max_species is expand's species budget. Either sets status truncated. polymerization is infinite: with max_complex_size n it gives chains of 1..n agents and rings of 2..n (a monomer cannot bind itself because embeddings are injective).
    - Mass-action is the only law: Kappa rules carry stochastic rate constants and the flattened ODE is the mass-action system over complexes. No flow, no energies.

## Results

Kappa is a modelling language, so its "results" are of two kinds: what the
language makes possible, and the behaviour of the example models its authors
publish. Chemart reproduces the second kind and the network sizes of the
first; it does not reproduce the biological studies done in Kappa.

**A few rules, thousands of reactions.** Blinov et al. (2006) built a model of
early EGFR signalling that tracks every complex and phosphorylation pattern
the protein interactions allow. Written as rules, it generates a network of
"356 molecular species, which are connected through 3749 unidirectional
reactions"; an earlier model of the same interactions had tracked only 18
species. The model was written in BioNetGen, a rule-based language close to
Kappa. The KaDE paper's supplementary page lists it among its benchmarks
taken from the BioNetGen repository, with a Kappa version, and reports 356
species for it. Chemart's flattening of that file gives
exactly 356 species and 3,749 reactions from 23 rules (39 rule directions),
with complexes of up to 14 agents; the test marked `slow` checks all three
numbers and that every agent type is conserved. This is the combinatorial
blow-up Kappa exists to avoid writing out by hand.

**The ABC model.** The reference guide's figure 3 shows a KaSim run of the ABC
model: unmodified C "drops rapidly and is replaced, at first, by simply
modified Cs ..., which are in turn replaced by doubly modified Cs", and the
AB complexes stabilise "slightly below 400 individuals after about 20s".
Chemart's deterministic version shows the same sequence (the table under
*Using it*: AB at 378 at 20 s and 382 afterwards; C almost entirely doubly
modified by 250 s). The tests check the exact set of 11 reactions and their
rates, that AB stays between 350 and 400 from 20 s on, that `Cpu` rises then
falls, and that more than 99% of C ends doubly modified. They also check that
the guide's rules in edit notation, taken from the KappaTools example file,
give the identical network. The 10-species, 11-reaction count is not printed
in any source; it was derived by hand from the five rules and agrees with the
generator.

**Dimers versus polymers.** The guide states that repeatedly applying the
symmetric rule "will result in a population of strict dimers", while the
asymmetric rule "will result in polymerization", with ring closure as its
unimolecular case. The tests check that the symmetric rule closes at monomer
and dimer, and that the polymerisation rule truncated at size n gives chains
of 1 to n agents, rings of 2 to n, n − 1 ring closures at rate 0.1 and the
expected number of joining reactions. No agent can bind itself, because an
embedding maps distinct pattern agents to distinct agents.

**Symmetry changes rates.** The guide argues that under stance D rule `'1p'`
has twice the activity of `'2p'`, and twice its own activity under stance ND.
The tests check all three stances for these two rules, and the guide's
homodimerisation example. One discrepancy: the guide's prose gives both rules
activity k/2 under stance ND, but its own equations give k (two embeddings,
each weighted by 1/2). Chemart follows the equations; the ratios the guide
states hold either way.

**What Chemart does not reproduce.** It does not implement KaSim's
continuous-time Monte Carlo over the site graph, which never enumerates
species and so can simulate models whose networks are infinite or too large
to list. Chemart must flatten first, and cuts infinite networks with its size
budgets. It does not implement agent creation or deletion (so it cannot model
synthesis or degradation), tokens, counters, rate functions, or KaDE's model
reduction by equivalent sites. It does not reproduce the original algebraic
syntax of Danos and Laneve (2004), with its visible and hidden free sites
(which could be written as an internal state), nor that paper's results on
self-assembly, its encoding of the calculus into a lower-level language of
binary interactions and into the π-calculus. The lactose operon and signalling
examples of that paper are not included.
